title: Expose separate path and content identities for rename continuity

state.decision_rationale: Rejected as redundant wire syntax. MKTCTX already keeps path-derived file IDs separate from full source SHA-256 identities, while Git change records supply rename evidence. Citation design should use those existing identities rather than add C-prefixed aliases.

provenance.review_target: Reported 39479-line MKTCTX/3 packet; exact artifact not identified

feedback.verbatim: Path-hashed F-IDs die on rename even when bytes are identical. Consider a dual ID: F<path-hash> plus C<content-hash> so agents can track a file across renames and packets.
feedback.normalized_claim: Give consumers explicit shorthand identities for both resource path and content bytes so they can distinguish renames, copies, edits, and aliases across packets.

current_behavior: F IDs derive from normalized packet paths, so a rename produces a new file ID by design.
Every index record already carries a full SHA-256 content digest, which supplies content identity without a C-prefixed shorthand.
Alias records represent byte-identical files within one packet by pointing to a canonical file body.
No cross-packet rename relation or VCS provenance is currently encoded.

proposal.summary: Evaluate whether a compact content ID improves citation and rename continuity beyond the existing full digest, while keeping path resources and byte identity categorically distinct.
candidate_changes: Define C IDs as collision-checked content-hash prefixes or reuse full sha256 as the normative content identity.
Specify citation and relation forms for renamed, copied, modified, and aliased files across packet identities.
Use VCS rename evidence when available rather than inferring rename solely from equal bytes.
Test prefix collision extension and distinguish multiple paths sharing one content identity.
non_goals: Do not make content identity replace path identity; identical bytes can be different resources.
Do not infer historical rename causality from equality alone.
Do not duplicate the full digest with a shorthand unless navigation or token savings justify it.

questions: What consumer operation becomes simpler with C IDs than with the existing sha256 field?
Should content IDs address raw bytes, canonical decoded text, or projection bytes?
How should citations distinguish a resource version from reusable content?
risks: A content ID can encourage consumers to collapse distinct paths or roles.
Short prefixes need collision detection and extension rules.
Encoding-exactness decisions can change the content-identity preimage.
evidence_needed: Rename, copy, edit, and alias test matrices across packet generations.
Consumer prototypes using full digests versus C-prefixed shorthand.
Collision handling and durable citation grammar tests.
